channel.title: Role cards :: School-related IT Infrastructure
channel.description: Each role card describes what has to run at the end, not how every click looks. You find the way there as a team with the official documentation (section Entry points). Exactly this way is what you record in the role runbook: a runbook that is only copied from the book helps nobody in an emergency. Every card has the same sections: Section Content The role at a school What the role is for, with an example from everyday school life Dependencies Which other roles have to run first Goal in the Windows world / Goal in the Linux world What runs at the end of session 1 (on its own, without a domain) Goal in session 2 How the role works together with the others Acceptance tests How you prove from the test client that it works Pitfalls What usually goes wrong Entry points Official documentation (primary sources) Comparison questions Questions for the runbook and the presentation Status: untested The commands, package names and menu items on the role cards have not yet been run in the Proxmox lab. Software as of November 2026 (Windows Server 2025, Debian 13 “trixie”). Check versions and commands in the official documentation. Tested on: open.

item.title: Team 1: DHCP
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.10, Windows DHCP server · Linux world: 10.50.13.21, Kea DHCPv4 (Debian container) The role at a school On the first day of school, 25 students open their laptops and all of them are on the network immediately. Nobody types in an IP address. The DHCP server gives every device an address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server, and remembers whom it “lent” what (lease). In real school networks every VLAN has its own range, and the router forwards the requests to a central server via DHCP relay (see chapter 3).

item.title: Team 2: DNS
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.11, Windows DNS server · Linux world: 10.50.13.22, BIND 9 (Debian container) The role at a school Teachers type moodle.schule.lan or drucker-lehrerzimmer, not 10.50.13.15. The DNS server translates names into addresses (and back) and forwards all other queries to the internet. Without DNS, almost nothing works at a Windows school: logging in to the domain finds the domain controller via DNS.

item.title: Team 3: Directory service
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.12, Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) · Linux world: 10.50.13.23, Samba as an Active Directory domain controller (Debian VM) This team has three people because almost all other roles wait for you in session 2. The role at a school A teacher logs in with one account on the computer in the staff room, in the computer lab and on the projector PC. Her class folder is there everywhere, so is the printer, and when she leaves the school, the administration locks one account instead of twenty. That is what a directory service does: a central list of users, groups and devices, with login (Kerberos), queries (LDAP) and policies. In Austria, at many schools this is an Active Directory.

item.title: Team 4: File shares
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.13, SMB shares with NTFS permissions · Linux world: 10.50.13.24, Samba (Debian container) The role at a school The class teacher puts worksheets into Klassen\3B; the students of 3B may read them but not delete them. Every teacher has a personal folder nobody else sees, and the administration has a drive that is invisible to teachers. These are shares (who gets to the folder over the network) and file permissions (who may do what inside it). The rules are written down in a permission matrix (see VLAN and permission matrices).

item.title: Team 5: Printing
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.14, print server · Linux world: 10.50.13.25, CUPS (Debian container) The role at a school There is a multifunction device in the staff room and a second one in the computer lab. Teachers should be able to print on both, students only in the computer lab, and at the end of the month the head wants to know how many pages were printed. A print server accepts the jobs of all devices, provides the drivers, controls who may print, and collects jobs in a queue.

item.title: Team 6: Web
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.15, Internet Information Services (IIS) · Linux world: 10.50.13.26, nginx (Debian container) The role at a school The intranet with the substitution plan, the sign-up page for parent–teacher days, the Moodle learning platform, the printer’s web interface: a school runs many websites that should only be reachable in its own network. A web server delivers them, often several sites on one server, distinguished by name (virtual hosts), and encrypted with HTTPS.

item.title: Team 7: Client deployment
item.description: FOG Project: 10.50.13.27 (Debian VM) · Windows reference machine: 10.50.13.16 · two empty target machines (VMs without an operating system) The role at a school End of August: 25 computers in the computer lab, carrying a school year’s worth of traces from 300 students. Instead of reinstalling each computer individually, you set up one computer cleanly (reference machine), take an image of it and play it over the network onto all the others at the same time. For this, the computers boot from the network (PXE), fetch a small boot program and write the image to their disk.

item.title: Team 8: Remote access
item.description: Windows world: 10.50.13.17, Remote Desktop (RDP) · Linux world: 10.50.13.28, OpenSSH and xrdp (Debian container) The role at a school The IT custodian is at home, and a service on the server in the basement has hung. Instead of driving to school, they connect over the network. Or: students work from weak laptops on a powerful server with programs they cannot install themselves. Both are remote access: as a command line (SSH, PowerShell remoting) for administration and as a graphical desktop (RDP) for working with programs.
